name: Chain-termination DNA sequencing
summary: Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson read DNA by copying it with chain-stopping nucleotides and sorting the fragments by length, the method that dominated DNA sequencing for decades.
description: Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson generated base-specific terminated extension products using nucleotide analogues and read the size-separated products on gels.
tier_reason: The reusable sequencing method underlies later automated sequencing and genome production across molecular research and medicine.

date.label: by 3 October 1977
date.basis: Method demonstrated by contribution on 3 October 1977; December publication is a later report milestone.

events.statement: Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson generated base-specific terminated extension products using nucleotide analogues and read the size-separated products on gels.
events.caveats: The paper used both dideoxy and arabino analogues and credited earlier inhibitor chemistry; it is not credited with the first φX174 genome report.

events.statement: Hamlyn and colleagues used an adaptation of the Sanger–Nicklen–Coulson method to sequence an immunoglobulin cDNA.
events.caveats: The 1978 work adapted the method for cDNA and shares the Cambridge MRC laboratory setting with the originating team; it is not proof of identical reagents, first outside use, or an independent institution.

links.statement: Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson presented chain termination as a further polymerase sequencing method related to plus/minus.
links.alternatives: Maxam–Gilbert chemical cleavage and Barnes ribosubstitution are acknowledged contemporary alternatives.
links.caveats: The new assay also depends on inhibitor chemistry; the plus/minus method is not its sole antecedent.
links.timing: Earlier plus/minus development is distinct from the later 1977 method.
